subject: Religionskunskap
title: The branches of Christianity
sourceSummary: Christianity's three main branches — Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant — and what separates them, the 16th-century Reformation and its consequences, sacraments and worship, the Church of Sweden and the free churches, and what Christianity looks like in the world today.
topics: the Church of Sweden and the free churches

questions.prompt: What are Christianity's three largest branches?
questions.opener: Two of them split apart in the year 1054, the third emerged in the 16th century.
choices: The Catholic Church, the Orthodox Church and the Protestant churches
The Catholic Church, Sunni and Shia
The Orthodox Church, the Church of Sweden and Judaism
Baptists, Methodists and Pentecostals
questions.explanation: Christianity is usually divided into three main branches. The Great Schism of 1054 split the church into a western, Catholic part and an eastern, Orthodox part, and the Reformation in the 16th century led to the Protestant churches emerging. The last option lists three denominations that are all Protestant free churches — they are thus branches within one of the three traditions, not three separate traditions. Sunni and Shia are, moreover, branches within Islam, not within Christianity.

questions.prompt: Which difference between the Catholic and Orthodox churches is correct?
questions.opener: Think about who is the church's highest leader in each tradition.
choices: The Orthodox Church is led by a pope, while the Catholic Church is led by several patriarchs
The Catholic Church has the Pope in Rome as its highest leader, while the Orthodox Church consists of several self-governing churches led by patriarchs and bishops
The Catholic Church uses no images at all, while the Orthodox Church requires all priests to live in celibacy
The Orthodox Church arose in the 16th century through the Reformation
questions.explanation: The Pope, who is the Bishop of Rome, is the head of the Catholic Church. The Orthodox Church is instead a communion of self-governing national churches, for example the Greek Orthodox and Russian Orthodox churches, where the Patriarch of Constantinople holds a position of honour but not the same decision-making power as the Pope. The third option is close to the opposite of the truth: icons hold a very central place in Orthodox worship, and Orthodox parish priests are allowed to marry, while priests in the Catholic Latin Church live in celibacy.

questions.prompt: What was the Reformation about, and who is usually considered its most famous figure?
questions.opener: The year 1517 and a German monk are usually mentioned first.
choices: Charlemagne had himself crowned emperor and founded a new church
The Council of Nicaea decided which scriptures should be included in the Bible

Martin Luther criticised, among other things, the sale of indulgences and argued that the Bible, not the church's traditions, should be the highest authority — which led to Protestant churches emerging
The Pope decided that all churches in Europe should be merged into a single one
questions.explanation: The Reformation is usually dated from the year 1517, when Martin Luther made his theses public in Wittenberg, criticising, among other things, the letters of indulgence, which were said to shorten time in purgatory. Luther emphasised that the Bible should be the highest authority and that, in his interpretation, humans are saved through faith, not through deeds or money. The option about Nicaea describes a church council in the 4th century, that is, more than a thousand years earlier, and has nothing to do with the Reformation.

questions.prompt: How does the view of sacraments differ between the Catholic Church and most Protestant churches?
questions.opener: Count the number — it differs between the two traditions.
choices: The Protestant churches have seven sacraments, while the Catholic Church has two
Neither tradition recognises any sacraments at all
Both have exactly the same three sacraments: baptism, confession and funerals
The Catholic Church has seven sacraments, while most Protestant churches recognise two: baptism and communion
questions.explanation: The Catholic Church recognises seven sacraments: baptism, confirmation, the eucharist (communion), confession, marriage, ordination and the anointing of the sick. Most Protestant churches count only baptism and communion as sacraments, since they hold that these are the two that Jesus himself instituted according to the gospels. The Orthodox Church has seven corresponding sacred acts, often called mysteries. Funerals are not counted as a sacrament in either tradition, which makes the third option wrong.

questions.topic: the Church of Sweden and the free churches
questions.prompt: What characterises the free churches in Sweden compared with the Church of Sweden?
questions.opener: The word "free" refers to the relationship to the state and the state church.
choices: The free churches are Catholic congregations that answer to the Pope in Rome

The free churches are Protestant denominations that grew up outside the state church, often emphasising personal faith, individual decision and strong member involvement — for example the Pentecostal movement and the Uniting Church in Sweden
Under Swedish law, the free churches are not allowed to hold their own services
The free churches are another name for the Church of Sweden's rural congregations
questions.explanation: The free churches grew out of the 19th-century revival movements alongside the then state church, and examples include the Pentecostal movement, the Uniting Church in Sweden, the Swedish Evangelical Free Church and the Swedish Alliance Mission. They often emphasise personal faith and an individual decision to belong to the congregation, and several practise believer's baptism of young people and adults, while the Church of Sweden, which is Evangelical Lutheran, usually baptises infants. The free churches are thus Protestant and are not under the Pope. The Church of Sweden remains Sweden's largest faith community, but has been separated from the state since the year 2000.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Christianity in the world today is most accurate?
questions.opener: Think about where most Christians live — and whether that is where the religion originally arose.
choices: Christianity in practice survives only in Europe
All Christians in the world belong to the same church and follow the same order of worship
Christianity is numerically the world's largest religion, and today most Christians live outside Europe — including in Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and North America
Christianity is the smallest of the five world religions
questions.explanation: With around 2.3–2.4 billion adherents, Christianity is the largest religion by number of followers. The centre of gravity has shifted markedly: the number of Christians is growing rapidly in sub-Saharan Africa and in parts of Asia, while the share of actively practising Christians in Europe has declined. Christianity is, moreover, divided into a great many denominations with different forms of worship, from quiet high mass to lively worship music — so the option about a single shared church and order of worship is not correct.

questions.prompt: Explain step by step how the Reformation unfolded and what consequences it had, both in Europe and in Sweden.
questions.opener: Follow the chain: the criticism, the spread, the split and the consequences in Sweden.
questions.answer: The background was widespread criticism of the Catholic Church's wealth and position of power, and especially of the letters of indulgence, which were sold with the promise of shortened time in purgatory. In 1517, the monk and theologian Martin Luther made his 95 theses public in Wittenberg, questioning the sale of indulgences. Luther held that the Bible, not the church's traditions or the Pope's authority, should be the highest guide, and that, in his interpretation, humans are saved through faith. Thanks to the printing press, his writings spread quickly across Europe, and the Bible began to be translated into the vernacular languages so that more people could read it themselves. The church in Western Europe split: Lutheran, Reformed (Calvinist) and Anglican churches emerged, while the Catholic Church responded with its own Counter-Reformation through the Council of Trent. The consequences were both religious and political — several countries were drawn into religious wars during the 16th and 17th centuries, and princes who joined the Reformation could take over the church's property and strengthen their own power. In Sweden, Gustav Vasa pushed through the Reformation from 1527, when the Riksdag in Västerås gave the Crown the right to the church's property; the New Testament appeared in Swedish in 1526 and the whole Bible in 1541. Sweden became Evangelical Lutheran, which was confirmed at the Uppsala Synod of 1593, and the church became closely tied to the state — a link that lasted right up until the year 2000. In the longer run, the Reformation's emphasis on everyone being able to read the Bible contributed to increased literacy in Sweden.
steps: Background: criticism of the Catholic Church's wealth, position of power and sale of letters of indulgence.
1517: Martin Luther makes his 95 theses public in Wittenberg and argues that the Bible, not the church's traditions, is the highest authority.
Spread: the printing press spreads the writings, and the Bible is translated into the vernacular languages.
Split in Europe: Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican churches are formed, the Catholic Church responds with the Counter-Reformation, and religious wars follow.

Sweden: Gustav Vasa pushes through the Reformation from 1527, the Bible appears in Swedish in 1541, the country becomes Evangelical Lutheran at the Uppsala Synod of 1593, and the church is tied to the state until the year 2000.

questions.prompt: Summarise the branches of Christianity: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, the Reformation, sacraments, the Church of Sweden and the free churches, and Christianity in the world.
questions.opener: Compare the three branches first, then take the history and the situation today.
questions.answer: Common to all Christians: belief in one God · Jesus as the Christ · the Bible (Old and New Testaments) as sacred scripture · baptism and communion · Three main branches: Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant · The Catholic Church: the Pope in Rome as head · seven sacraments · the mass at the centre · priests in the Latin Church live in celibacy · largest in the world by number of followers · The Orthodox Church: self-governing national churches (Greek, Russian, Serbian Orthodox and others) · the Patriarch of Constantinople holds a position of honour · icons and liturgy are central · parish priests are allowed to marry · The Protestant churches: the Bible as the highest authority · usually two sacraments (baptism and communion) · preaching at the centre · no claims to a pope · The Schism of 1054: the church splits into East and West · The Reformation of 1517: Luther's theses against the sale of indulgences → Protestant churches, printing, Bible translations, religious wars, the Counter-Reformation (Trent) · Sweden: Gustav Vasa from 1527 · the Bible in Swedish in 1541 · the Uppsala Synod of 1593 · The Church of Sweden: Evangelical Lutheran, the largest faith community, infant baptism, separated from the state in the year 2000 · Free churches: out of the 19th-century revival — the Pentecostal movement, the Uniting Church in Sweden and others · personal faith, often believer's baptism, strong member involvement · Globally: around 2.3–2.4 billion Christians · most now live outside Europe, with rapid growth in sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia.
